allowedSourceMaterial.overview: When news of John Smith's death reaches America, Pocahontas is devastated. She sets off to London with John Rolfe, to meet with the King of England on a diplomatic mission: to create peace and respect between the two great lands. However, Governor Ratcliffe is still around; he wants to return to Jamestown and take over. He will stop at nothing to discredit the young princess.

visibleEditorialCopy.curiosityHook: With Governor Ratcliffe plotting to humiliate her before the English court, can Pocahontas secure peace before his schemes prevail?
visibleEditorialCopy.description: Grieving the reported death of John Smith, Pocahontas travels to London alongside John Rolfe on a royal peace mission, only to face Governor Ratcliffe's ruthless plot to sabotage her standing with the King.
visibleEditorialCopy.vibeSummary: An easy-watching, moderately emotional animated adventure with steady pace and lively court intrigue.
visibleEditorialCopy.whyWatch: Running a swift 72 minutes, this animated adventure blends royal intrigue and romantic drama into a spirited, accessible family journey across the Atlantic.

claudeAdvisory.claimSpan: plotting to humiliate her before the English court
issueSummaries: description says Ratcliffe's plot is 'to sabotage her standing with the King', and curiosityHook says he is 'plotting to humiliate her before the English court'. The overview says only that he 'will stop at nothing to discredit the young princess' and that he wants to return to Jamestown and take over. It does not say the plot targets the King, takes place at court, or unfolds in London. The copy therefore specifies the audience, venue and mechanism of the scheme, and it ties Ratcliffe to the diplomatic mission in a way the packet does not state. 'Humiliate' is also a different act from 'discredit'.
claudeAdvisory.sourceBoundaryReason: Most of the copy is grounded or is tolerated figurative language and genre shorthand under A_PRIME_PRODUCTION_MATERIALITY_V1. The concern is the way description and curiosityHook stage Ratcliffe's scheme: its target (the King), its venue (the English court) and its form (public humiliation or sabotage of her standing). The overview says only that he will discredit the princess and wants to take over Jamestown. These additions falsely specify plot mechanics and the scheme's setting, which are named materiality categories, and they shape viewer expectations of the film's central conflict. They do not contradict the source, invent identities, or reveal an outcome or ending, so the severity is MINOR and not SEVERE. A bounded fix would stay with the overview's own wording, for example 'Governor Ratcliffe, who wants to take over Jamestown, will stop at nothing to discredit the young princess'.

sourceEvidence.notes: description and curiosityHook: 'sabotage her standing with the King' and 'humiliate her before the English court' have no support. The overview gives Ratcliffe's goals as returning to Jamestown and taking over, and his method as discrediting the princess, without naming who is to be convinced or where. The King appears only as the person Pocahontas is meeting.

description: grieving the news of John Smith's death ('reported' preserves the source's 'news of'), the trip to London with John Rolfe, the royal peace mission, and Governor Ratcliffe's plot against her all restate the overview. 'Ruthless' paraphrases 'will stop at nothing'. 'Royal peace mission' paraphrases 'diplomatic mission... peace and respect'.

curiosityHook: 'can Pocahontas secure peace' restates the mission to create peace and respect. 'Before his schemes prevail' is figurative urgency in the class of the tolerated 'before mom returns'. The interrogative asserts no outcome.

whyWatch: 'animated adventure', 'romantic drama' and 'family journey' are consistent with genres Adventure/Animation/Family/Romance. '72 minutes' matches runtimeMinutes. 'Across the Atlantic' follows from a trip from America to London. 'Royal intrigue' is thematic shorthand for the King, the princess and the governor's scheming.

claudeAdvisory.uncertaintyNotes: This is a near-threshold call. The overview places the discrediting right after the London mission, so a reader would probably infer that the court is the arena, and 'discredit' does imply damage to her reputation. An adjudicator could treat 'sabotage her standing with the King' as a natural gloss on 'discredit the young princess' and approve. I flag the fields because the packet never says the plot targets the King or happens in London, and because 'court' recurs in vibeSummary ('court intrigue') and in whyWatch ('royal intrigue'). I left those two within tolerance as atmospheric shorthand, though a stricter reading could extend the concern to them. 'Only to face' implies Ratcliffe is present on the trip, which the overview does not say, since he 'is still around' and wants to return to Jamestown. I did not treat that as a separate issue.

geminiAdvisory.sourceBoundaryReason: All visible editorial copy strictly complies with A_PRIME_PRODUCTION_MATERIALITY_V1. The narrative premise, diplomatic mission, and Ratcliffe's antagonistic plot in the description and curiosityHook adhere faithfully to the authorized overview. Crucially, the copy exercises rigorous setup-only restraint by qualifying John Smith's status as 'reported death' and omitting third-act revelations regarding his survival or subsequent relationship choices between Smith and Rolfe. Framing phrases such as 'royal peace mission' and 'court intrigue' represent legitimate, low-risk contextual concretization and genre shorthand anchored in the authorized meeting with the King of England.
